newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: SIMEX's dormant fuel oil contract is revived.
newsitem.headline: SIMEX's dormant fuel oil contract is revived.

text.p: The Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) launched its new-look fuel oil futures contract on Tuesday in a bid to revive the long dormant market.
Trading started on an open-outcry basis at 0630 GMT with a flurry of initial deals.
By 1010 GMT, 20,000 tonnes of fuel oil had changed hands on the exchange and all the trades had taken place in the first hour of trading, market figures showed.
SIMEX President Ang Swee Tian said he hoped the contract would be successful.
"We have started it in response to what the energy trading community wants," he told reporters at the official launch.
"When we changed the contract's specfications, we did so in response to what the trading community wanted. Ultimately we leave it to the market to decide whether it will work, Swee said.
SIMEX has listed a fuel oil contract since 1989, but it has been untraded since 1995 when the specifications of the contract fell out of line with the physical market.
SIMEX already provides an open-outcry market to trade North Sea Brent futures and plans to revive a gas oil contract after one failed to take off earlier in the 1990s.
Traders gave the new look fuel oil contract a cautious seal of approval but said the recent failings of futures energy contracts on SIMEX could keep users on the sidelines initially.
But most traders welcomed having an alternative hedging tool to the over-the-counter swaps derivatives.

They said fuel oil futures would provide greater price transparency, as Asia energy markets tend to be secretive with trades in both physical oil and derivatives taking place over the counter and generally only between two parties at a time.
"The exchange is regulated and therefore I think, unlike the swaps market, there would be less room for manipulation," said a Chinese trader at the launch. He declined to be identified.
He said China has suspended oil futures trading, so his company had been seeking a viable exchange in Asia to hedge and buy physical fuel oil.
But some oil traders said they were concerns the new contract, like the initial contract, would just fizzle out.

Tim Bullock, regional products trading manager for British Petroleum (Far East) said unless the futures market picks up good liquidity quickly, trade was likely to stay with the alternative swaps derivative market.
David Short, managing director of Dutch trader Vitol, said Asia's potential for growth could provide room for both a futures and a swaps market.

"At the moment, Asia is a cash orientated market. Swaps and future volume lags behind the physical market. If SIMEX is able to attract new volume and enhance the oil trade in Singapore that would be a benefit," he said.
